title: How long does Apple support iPads? iPadOS 27, security updates and repair support
content:
Macworld





If you own an older iPad – or are considering buying a refurbished iPad – you may be wondering how long Apple will continue to support it and whether you should update to a newer model. 
Apple has one of the best software support records in the industry. Many iPads receive major iPadOS updates for six to eight years, and some continue to receive security updates even after they stop getting new features.
As of September 2026, iPads that can run iPadOS 27 receive Apple’s current operating system and are fully supported. Some older models that cannot upgrade to iPadOS 27 are still receiving security updates through older versions of iPadOS. Eventually every device reaches a point where Apple stops providing software updates and hardware repairs though.
Here’s what you need to know about how long iPads remain supported, when it’s time to upgrade, and which older models are still worth buying.


Does Apple support my iPad?
Fully supported iPads can run the latest version of iPadOS, currently iPadOS 27.
Apple’s iPadOS 27 compatibility list includes the 4th-generation 12.9-inch Pro, 2nd-generation 11-inch Pro, 4th-generation Air, 9th-generation iPad and 6th-generation mini.
Unfortunately, iPadOS 27 dropped support for:
iPad Pro 12.9-inch (3rd generation)
iPad Pro 11-inch (1st generation)
iPad Air (3rd generation)
iPad (8th generation)
iPad mini (5th generation)
Those models have not been abandoned, however. Apple released iPadOS 26.7 on September 14 and iPadOS 26.7.1 on September 28 for the iPads that cannot move to iPadOS 27. 
Older models that cannot run the latest release may continue to receive security updates for several years. However, once Apple stops providing security patches, users may encounter increasing security risks and app compatibility problems.
Apple may continue providing security updates for devices that can no longer run the latest iPadOS for several years. For example, the 7th-generation iPad still receives iPadOS 18 security updates, with iPadOS 18.7.10 released on August 17, 2026. The 2nd-generation iPad Pro and 6th-generation iPad run iPadOS 17, which was updated to version 17.7.11 in May 2026. Apple also issued security updates for iPadOS 16 and iPadOS 15 at the same time. 
Apple does not promise how long it will maintain each older version of iPadOS. The arrival of iPadOS 27 has already shifted the support picture: iPadOS 26 remains supported for devices that cannot upgrade to iPadOS 27, while the 7th-generation iPad remains on the iPadOS 18 security branch. If your iPad can no longer run the latest version of iPadOS and is no longer receiving security updates, it is nearing the end of its practical lifespan.
Check the chart below to see whether your iPad can run iPadOS 27 or is still receiving security updates.

				
					

				
			
The iPads supported by iPadOS
..

Foundry



							


How long does Apple support iPads?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Apple doesn’t publish a fixed support timetable for iPads, but historically many models have received around six to eight years of major operating-system updates, followed in some cases by additional years of security updates. The precise lifespan varies by model. 
With iPadOS 27, the oldest supported Pro generation is the 2020 iPad Pro: the 11-inch 2nd generation and 12.9-inch 4th generation.
Support generally falls into two stages:
Major iPadOS updates
Most iPads receive new versions of iPadOS for several years after launch. These updates include new features, interface changes and compatibility improvements.
Devices that support the latest version of iPadOS – currently iPadOS 27 – are considered fully supported. Devices that support iPadOS 27 receive Apple’s current operating system, although some individual features have newer hardware requirements. 
Security updates
Even after an iPad stops receiving major feature updates, Apple often continues to provide security patches for older versions of iPadOS.
These updates fix vulnerabilities, maintain compatibility with Apple’s services and help extend the safe lifespan of older devices.
For many iPads, security support continues for years after major software support ends.
Apple continues to issue security updates for several older iPadOS versions. As of September 2026, the clearest examples are iPadOS 26.7.1 for iPads dropped by iPadOS 27, and iPadOS 18.7.10 for the 7th-generation iPad. Apple also periodically patches still older systems for older hardware.


						

							


Why security updates matter: The risks of using an unsupported iPad

				
					

				
			
Britta O’Boyle




Security updates are particularly important because they protect your data and device from newly discovered vulnerabilities.
Without security updates, an iPad becomes increasingly exposed to threats and may eventually lose compatibility with essential services.
An iPad that still receives security updates can remain suitable for many everyday tasks.
Once an iPad stops receiving security updates, it becomes increasingly difficult to recommend using it for anything involving personal information.
Potential issues include:
Security vulnerabilities that are never patched
Banking and payment apps ceasing to work
App Store compatibility problems
Loss of support for services such as FaceTime and iMessage
Difficulty activating or restoring the device
Reduced performance and battery life
Unsupported devices may continue functioning, but their usefulness declines over time.


						

							


Which iPads support iPadOS 27?

				
					

				
			
Apple




These iPads are compatible with iPadOS 27 and are considered fully supported:
iPad Pro 12.9-inch (4th generation and later)
iPad Pro 11-inch (2nd generation and later)
iPad Pro 13-inch (M4 and later)
iPad Air (4th generation and later)
iPad (9th generation and later)
iPad mini (6th generation and later)


						

							


Which iPads are stuck on iPadOS 26 but still get security updates?
Some iPads that cannot upgrade to iPadOS 27 are still receiving security updates through iPadOS 26. Apple released iPadOS 26.7.1 on September 28, 2026, for these older models.
The iPads that are limited to iPadOS 26 include:
iPad Pro 12.9-inch (3rd generation)
iPad Pro 11-inch (1st generation)
iPad Air (3rd generation)
iPad (8th generation)
iPad mini (5th generation)
These iPads no longer receive the major new features introduced in iPadOS 27, but Apple is continuing to provide security updates for them.


						

							


What about older iPads that can’t run iPadOS 26?
Some older iPads are still receiving security updates even though they cannot run either iPadOS 27 or iPadOS 26.
For example, Apple released iPadOS 18.7.10 on August 17, 2026, specifically for the 7th-generation iPad.
Other, even older iPads may occasionally receive security updates for earlier versions of iPadOS, but these updates are less frequent and shouldn’t be taken as a guarantee of ongoing support.


						

							


When does Apple stop repairing iPads?

				
					

				
			
Dominik Tomaszewski/IDG




Software support isn’t the only factor that determines an iPad’s lifespan. Apple also classifies older devices as Vintage or Obsolete based on how long ago it stopped distributing them for sale.
These classifications relate primarily to hardware repairs and parts availability, rather than iPadOS support. An iPad can therefore be classified as vintage while still receiving software or security updates.
Vintage products
Products become Vintage when Apple stopped distributing them for sale more than five years ago but less than seven years ago. Repairs may still be available, subject to parts availability.
Vintage iPads
Apple currently classifies the following iPads as vintage:
iPad Air (Cellular models)
iPad Air (3rd generation)
iPad Pro 10.5-inch
iPad Pro 11-inch (1st generation)
iPad Pro 12.9-inch (3rd generation)
iPad (6th generation)
Certain older iPad Wi-Fi + 4G models
Obsolete products
Products become obsolete when Apple stopped distributing them for sale more than seven years ago. Apple then discontinues hardware service, and Apple-authorized service providers can no longer order replacement parts.
Obsolete iPads
Original iPad
iPad 2
iPad (3rd generation)
iPad (4th generation)
iPad (5th generation)
iPad Air
iPad Air 2
iPad mini
iPad mini 2
iPad mini 3
iPad mini 4
iPad Pro 9.7-inch
iPad Pro 12.9-inch (1st generation)
iPad Pro 12.9-inch (2nd generation)


						

							





 FAQ 


1.
How many years do iPads get updates?
Most iPads receive major iPadOS updates for approximately six to eight years, with security support often continuing beyond that.





2.
Is an old iPad still safe to use?
An older iPad that continues to receive Apple security updates is considerably safer to use than one that no longer receives patches, although app and service support may still decline as the device ages.





3.
Can I use an iPad after Apple stops supporting it?
Yes, but you may encounter security risks, app compatibility problems and hardware repair limitations.





4.
Which versions of iPadOS does Apple support with security updates?
Apple provides security updates for the current version of iPadOS and may continue to patch older versions for devices that cannot upgrade. As of September 2026, Apple is providing iPadOS 26.7.1 for models that cannot run iPadOS 27, while the 7th-generation iPad has received iPadOS 18.7.10. Apple also occasionally issues security updates for still older versions, but it does not publish a fixed support timetable.





5.
What is Apple’s oldest supported iPad?
It depends what you mean by supported. The oldest iPads receiving the latest iPadOS are newer than some models that continue to receive security-only updates. Apple also occasionally issues security fixes for much older devices, so the oldest model receiving some form of support can change when new patches are released.





6.
How can I find out how old my iPad is? 
To identify your iPad:
Open Settings 
Go to General 
Tap on About 
Find the Model Name
You can then compare your model with the list above to see what year that iPad was introduced.





7.
Why do some iPads lose support sooner than others
The processor and RAM inside an iPad plays a major role in determining how long it remains supported.
More powerful models generally remain compatible with new features for longer, while entry-level models tend to reach the end of software support sooner.
This is especially important as newer versions of iPadOS introduce increasingly demanding features and AI capabilities.





8.
Should I buy an older iPad?
A refurbished iPad can still be a good purchase, but we recommend choosing a model that supports the current version of iPadOS whenever possible. Read: Best place to buy a refurbished iPad.
If you’re planning to keep the iPad for several years, avoid models that are already limited to security updates only.
For most buyers, choosing an iPad released within the last two generations offers the best balance of performance, longevity and value.





Want to know how long Apple supports iPhones and how long Apple supports Macs, we have that covered too.

title: Siri may know a lot more, but it’s still not smart
content:
Macworld





After years of complaints about its limitations and poor overall performance, Siri finally received its long-overdue AI-centric overhaul with iOS 27. The virtual assistant now has a large language model (LLM) foundation, allowing it to comprehend natural speech and discuss a wider range of topics, uniquely analyze what’s visible on your screen, surface your personal data, and perform in-app actions when prompted.
But while Siri AI undoubtedly addresses many of our main issues with its knowledge, its position in iOS 27, while technically still in beta mode but very much available to everyone, introduces a whole new set of drawbacks. From questionable design decisions to lingering unreliability, the new Siri still has a long way to go.
Stealing the Spotlight
Spotlight Search was once one of the best tools to find any local file, launch apps, define words, run shortcuts, calculate, and much more. It was predictable, and it worked well; you swipe down anywhere on the Home Screen to reveal the search bar, start typing, and on-device results would instantly populate and update as you enter your keywords in real time. That was until Siri AI stole its spot and downgraded the entire system.
As of iOS 27, the same gesture reveals a Search or Ask field powered by Siri. Instead of immediately showing you a list of all relevant, on-device results, it now tends to highlight only one local item and prioritizes relaying your search query to Siri. You still get a button to show all results, but the overall workflow is now unintuitive and time-consuming. I often find myself quickly hitting search to locate something, only for Siri AI to take over and give me something I didn’t want.
I get why Apple decided to merge the two functionalities, but many users agree that Spotlight Search and Siri are two very different tools that serve unique purposes. Taking away Spotlight’s predictability defeats the point of the quick search feature. And don’t get me started on the smaller touch target for the Notification Center.

				
					

				
			
Siri intrudes on too many menus in iOS 27.

Foundry




Writing fools
Spotlight Search isn’t Siri AI’s only new home. iOS 27 also brings Writing Tools under the broader Siri umbrella, degrading the user experience in the process.
Since its initial debut a couple of years ago, I’ve actively relied on the Proofread feature to pinpoint typos and double spaces in my articles. Unlike asking an AI chatbot to proofread, it strictly amends language errors, sparing you from the infamous robotic recommendations and unwanted stylistic tweaks. It’s also less prone to hallucinating or skipping through the text.
With the latest update, Writing Tools are now part of the Write with Siri feature, which prioritizes generating text from scratch rather than simple editing. When I select a passage, the Proofread button doesn’t always show up—and manually asking Siri to proofread the selection gets me a subjective AI chatbot response rather than triggering the objective editing flow.
Even when the native Proofread button appears, its functionality has been botched. The system used to offer arrows to jump between applied edits to review and revert them as needed; I might be missing it, but it’s seemingly gone now, along with the change counter on macOS. So I have to carefully scan the entire text manually to detect the subtly underlined words where edits were made for the final revision. The whole thing is just unintuitive.
Pushy buttons
Siri AI’s takeover can be perceived across the entire system—beyond Spotlight Search and Writing Tools. You’ll notice there’s a new Ask Siri button in context menus all over iOS 27, a design choice that is both intrusive and nonsensical. Siri has a dedicated hardware button, a voice command trigger, and a new universal software gesture; it is accessible anywhere at any time through three distinct methods.
A simple splash screen or onboarding flow informing users about the assistant’s upgraded capabilities would’ve been sufficient for them to learn they can ask Siri about anything now. The same could be said about the new persistent Siri mode in the overloaded Camera app, when Visual Intelligence has long been accessible via the Control Center toggle, Action button, and Camera Control button.
Willful ignorance
Having lived abroad for half a decade, I often come across social media posts written in foreign languages. Prior to Siri AI’s launch, I’d simply its predecessor to have ChatGPT explain what’s on my screen. This would intuitively upload a screenshot to OpenAI’s servers and deliver the response through Siri’s native interface.
With iOS 27, you can still ask Siri for ChatGPT responses, but ChatGPT’s ability to see what’s on your screen is neutered. Given that Siri AI can now handle the task itself, one would shrug it off—except that Siri AI isn’t as smart as OpenAI’s offering.

				
					

				
			
Siri AI’s ability to translate, one of the things AI is supposed to be great at, leaves much to be desired. 

Foundry




When I ask Siri AI to analyze foreign text on an image and break down the context, it tends to bring up an instance of Apple Translate, which is exceptionally unreliable at understanding casual, online lingo. So, I need to repeatedly rephrase my prompt and beg Siri AI to eventually agree to analyze the text itself using its knowledge rather than Apple Translate. This adds unnecessary friction and complication to a feature that had long worked smoothly. Siri AI is perfectly capable of handling cultural nuances and foreign slang, and its LLM-powered responses should be the default for this type of request.
Severed servers
Have you missed classic Siri’s “I’m not sure I understand” responses? You’ll be delighted to learn that they live on through Siri AI’s “Something went wrong” error message. While the AI chatbot now does understand most queries, the service frequently gets interrupted and disconnects from Apple’s servers. This often forces you to start over a conversation, which is particularly problematic given that Siri AI cannot recall previous conversations or build and maintain a memory.
Beyond randomly slowing down or failing altogether, the Siri app itself feels half-baked. The interface isn’t as fluid as other native apps, and it sometimes silently defaults back to asking Siri while conversing with the in-app ChatGPT model. Other annoyances include repeatedly mishearing voice commands and asking for clarification on whether I meant X or Y—an issue I never encountered with the old Siri. The app could also use a true voice mode and fewer or more subtle “I’m an AI, please verify info” alerts.

				
					

				
			
It’s still in beta, of course, but Siri gets tripped up far too often.

Foundry




Whatcha say?
The Siri app’s poor performance is even worse when accessing it from your wrist. watchOS 27 infamously dropped support for all Apple Watches older than the Series 9—presumably to ensure fluidity. Nevertheless, Siri AI is almost unusable on all recent models, taking much longer than before to perform basic tasks and often failing completely. Given that complaints are all over the web, this certainly isn’t an isolated bug. Virtual assistants are designed to speed up life and make it easier, and sadly Siri AI is failing at its core purpose.

title: Apple under Ternus: More products, more often, with a ‘leaner’ staff
content:
Macworld





Stop me if you’ve heard this one before: Tech company’s new CEO thinks the company can do more with fewer people! That’s the gist of a new report from Mark Gurman at Bloomberg about the internal changes Apple is now going through after its first few weeks under new CEO John Ternus.
For investors, it all sounds like good news. For employees, it’s worrying. And for customers and Apple users, it’s a bit of a mixed bag.
The good news is that there’s a real effort to release more products. We’ve expected for some time that the first year of Ternus’ time as CEO would be packed with new products, not necessarily because of the new CEO, but just because a lot of products long rumored to be coming are finally nearing completion.
The folding iPhone Duo was just the start: There are touchscreen MacBooks, AirPods with cameras, smart glasses, a new smart home hub, and a 20th Anniversary iPhone all coming up in the next 12 months. And that’s in addition to regular updates to iPhone, iPad, and Mac product lines. However, that’s not enough for Ternus, according to Gurman’s wide-ranging report.
According to his sources, Apple’s new CEO wants the company to become “more experimental” and introduce new products more quickly. There’s definitely a double-edged sword to that philosophy: Most Apple fans want the company to take risks and big swings like iPhone Duo, but nobody wants to buy an Apple product that gets abandoned after a couple of years because it didn’t take off. Apple has always prided itself on its selectivity, so a focus on risk-taking is, in itself, risky.
Ternus also believes, according to the report, that Apple products should be released year-round, not just at a big event in the fall and the spring. That’s definitely a stance we can get behind.
The report says Ternus believes Apple can accomplish this accelerated, engineering-focused, bolder product roadmap while still becoming “leaner.” He believes Apple should hire fewer people and trim its bloated middle management. In the last couple of weeks, Gurman reports, Apple has begun dismissing engineering program managers (EPM), and multiple teams have been scaled back or reassigned as the company has carried out some small-scale layoffs.
Groups that have been reduced recently include the Siri team, Vision Pro headset, some AI-related software engineering, and Fitness+. Some of these are allegedly due to employee performance, while others are due to changes in direction for those products.
Worryingly, Ternus is said to have “explored how artificial intelligence could accelerate product development and perform work currently handled by employees,” which is in line with other big tech companies that have pushed to get more done with fewer people through the use of AI. So far, it hasn’t played out well, with many discovering that AI’s shortcomings have resulted in as much additional work as they save, and a lot of companies have had to re-hire many of those they have let go.
Apple had a plan to lay off some 5,000 AppleCare support personnel, many of whom work from home, thinking it could use AI phone and web support agents to handle a lot of support responsibilities. But the company “ultimately put those plans on hold and isn’t currently looking to take such a step,” Gurman reports.
However, Apple is looking to cut costs in other places. Previously planned budget or staffing increases, the article claims, have been held flat or reduced.
The most worrying part is the claim that the new CEO is looking for ways to not just sell more devices to more customers, but to increase revenue from existing customers. Services revenue, while still growing, has slowed lately, and the revenue generated by the App Store is in peril as Apple’s policies are under scrutiny worldwide. That means Apple may launch new services, increase prices for existing services, or find other ways to generate revenue from its products, such as adding ads to Apple Maps.
A new CEO always comes with a period of major change and adjustment for employees. As a customer, it’s hard not to be concerned about a company that plans to do more, faster, with fewer people. That’s usually a recipe for lower quality. But it’s also quite possible that Apple is bloated with middle management that doesn’t do much other than slow things down, and a leaner Apple could be beneficial to progress.
As the article cautions, many of Apple’s long-established product development practices could take years to change. But in the meantime, as one source told Gurman, it’s going to be “hectic” in Cupertino.

title: AirPods 5 Teardown: Batteries Removable, Case Still Tough
content:
Repair site iFixit today took apart Apple's AirPods 5 for one of its traditional teardown videos. It turns out the new AirPods are slightly more repairable than prior models, but it's still not a simple home fix.



The ‌AirPods 5‌ use pronged batteries that Apple previously used in the AirPods 3, but not the AirPods 4. The battery can be removed with a "nifty pair of tongs," and iFixit says the component is "intuitive to unplug." When the AirPods 3 used the pronged battery, there was no easy way to get into the earbud, but the ‌AirPods 5‌ are easier to pry open.

iFixit was able get into the ‌AirPods 5‌ with a hair dryer to heat the adhesive and a clamp to hold the earbud in place. The left and right earbuds use different batteries with reversed polarity, so the battery from a left AirPod can't be swapped into a right AirPod, and vice versa.

While the earbuds have a better repair score, iFixit said the case is "still a disaster" and difficult to get into without destroying it.

title: Apple Shares New Guide for Using iOS 27 Parental Controls
content:
Apple today shared a guide meant to help parents use the child safety tools in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS Golden Gate. Apple says "Building Healthy Digital Habits: A Guide for Families" was developed in partnership with the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP).


The six-step guide covers balancing screen time with sleep, exercise, schoolwork, and time with friends and family. It has advice on getting kids on board with screen time limits and using the different parental control features. From Apple's announcement:

 	
Start a conversation about screen time, with tips for parents to approach the topic and establish expectations in a way that helps kids feel included in the plan.

 	
Create a Child Account, which enables age-based safeguards and gives parents access to parental controls to manage their child's experience.

 	
Set safety settings for websites and apps, including Ask to Buy and Ask to Browse, so families can review new apps and websites together.

 	
Make a schedule for device use, using Time Allowances and Schedules to balance time online with sleep, schoolwork, physical activity, and time with family and friends.

 	
Manage communications, with parents deciding who their child can communicate with and Communication Safety, on by default for all users under 18, helping protect kids from viewing or sharing sensitive content.

 	
Continue the conversation as kids grow, with guidance on adjusting the family's plan over time.


The guide includes the AAP's recommendations on screen time by age group, from infants to teens, along with strategies to help children develop healthy screen time habits.

added new parental control options and an overhauled version of Screen Time in ‌iOS 27‌. Parents can choose which apps children can access, monitor and control website access, keep tabs on approved contacts, and set different screen time schedules based on time of day. Using the new version of Screen Time requires all devices in a Family Sharing group to be running ‌iOS 27‌, ‌iPadOS 27‌, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27.

title: Apple Creator Studio and Final Cut Camera Get New Features
content:
Apple today updated Apple Creator Studio and Final Cut Camera for iOS to add new features.


Final Cut Camera, Apple's professional iPhone filming app, now supports the variable aperture feature on the iPhone 18 Pro. Users can tweak aperture and select between aperture priority and shutter priority modes, plus there's support for Cinematic mode effects for video. Apple says the app was also redesigned from the ground up to give creators easy access to pro settings like shutter angle, ISO, and white balance.

There are customizable overlays with false color and clipping indicators for exposure and improved focus peaking with sensitivity control. title: Switch Siri AI for ChatGPT on Your Mac
content:
In macOS 27 Golden Gate, Siri AI is a lot smarter than before, so it doesn't always flail and attempt to hand your questions over to ChatGPT. However, if you still prefer OpenAI's chatbot for certain queries, you can still ask for it explicitly. 


In macOS Tahoe, Siri would suggest passing a request to ChatGPT when it thought the chatbot could help. In macOS 27 though, ChatGPT only answers when you specifically ask it. There's also no setting that makes ChatGPT your default assistant – as things stand, you need to choose it for each query. Here's how it's done.

Turn On the ChatGPT Extension


Open System Settings.

  
Click Siri in the sidebar.

  
Click ChatGPT under "Extension."

  
Turn on Use Extension.

  
Choose whether to sign in with a ChatGPT account.


If you sign in, your requests are saved to your ChatGPT chat history (OpenAI's privacy policies apply). If you skip sign-in, OpenAI receives nothing tied to your Apple Account and it can't store your requests.

Ask ChatGPT in Search or Ask


Press Command-Space to open the Search or Ask bar (formerly Spotlight Search).

title: AppleCare Guide: Is it Worth Paying For?
content:
Most Apple products come with a one-year limited warranty that covers hardware failures and manufacturing defects, and up to 90 days of complimentary technical support. To extend your coverage further, Apple offers AppleCare+ and AppleCare One, with theft and loss coverage available for eligible devices. With the added cost, service fees, and varying prices across the Apple product lineup, is AppleCare worth paying for?



Apple uses several similar names for different types of coverage:


Standard warranty: Included with most Apple products at no extra cost. It generally covers manufacturing defects for one year. It is not an AppleCare plan.

AppleCare: Apple's umbrella name for its paid service and support plans, rather than one specific level of coverage. The older AppleCare Protection Plan is a distinct product that still appears in some markets.

AppleCare+: A paid plan for one eligible product that extends hardware service and support and adds accidental damage coverage. Service fees apply to accidental damage claims.

AppleCare+ with Theft and Loss: Includes AppleCare+ benefits and adds theft and loss protection for eligible iPhones, iPads, and Apple Watches, subject to claim limits and deductibles.

AppleCare One: A monthly plan for multiple eligible products. Its Individual tier includes AppleCare+ benefits and theft and loss coverage for enrolled iPhones, iPads, and Apple Watches.

AppleCare One Family: Covers eligible products belonging to the subscriber and up to five other people in a Family Sharing group. It can also cover one person's devices without a Family Sharing group.



iPad, Apple Watch, Mac, or Apple TV. AppleCare One can also cover eligible devices you already own that are in good condition and within four years of their manufacture, purchase, or activation date, depending on the information Apple has. AirPods and Beats devices have a one-year limit.

added through AppleCare & Warranty settings on an iPhone, ‌iPad‌, Mac, or Apple Vision Pro, or purchased online. Monthly and annual plans renew while active until canceled. Fixed-term plans have a stated end date, after which further coverage may be available if the device qualifies.

Theft and loss protection is now available well beyond the initial markets of the United States and Japan, but eligible devices, prices, service fees, and claim rules differ by market. Before purchasing a plan, check the exact terms for your device where you live.

Standard Warranty

The standard warranty that comes free with your device is simply a limited warranty, which is very common for consumer devices. This warranty guarantees that the product will work as expected for up to a year. If something materially breaks within that timeframe, and it is through no fault of the user, Apple will fix it free of charge. This warranty is also automatically applied no matter where you buy the product.

The warranty does not cover accidental damage, cosmetic wear, or a battery that has worn down through normal use. Apple may ask for proof of purchase when arranging service. To transfer the warranty, you simply need to provide the buyer with your proof of purchase. Some limitations apply and the length of the standard warranty may vary based on your country. The warranty and AppleCare plans are in addition to rights provided by consumer law in your country.

AppleCare+

AppleCare+ provides paid coverage for one eligible product. Its principal benefits are:


Hardware service and priority technical support for the term of the plan.

Unlimited eligible accidental damage incidents, each subject to a service fee.

Battery service at no extra charge for devices with rechargeable batteries when capacity falls below 80%.

Express Replacement Service for eligible products, subject to its terms and availability.

Theft and loss protection on eligible "AppleCare+ with Theft and Loss" plans, subject to claim limits and deductibles.



Drops, spills, and broken screens are common examples of accidental damage. The damage must affect the device's function; ordinary wear and cosmetic damage are generally excluded. Eligible hardware faults arising after the limited warranty expires do not carry an additional repair fee.

cannot be transferred to a new owner.

AppleCare+ With Theft and Loss

AppleCare+ with Theft and Loss adds replacement coverage if an eligible iPhone, ‌iPad‌, or Apple Watch is lost or stolen. Other products, such as Macs, displays, headphones, ‌Apple TV‌, and HomePod, are only available with AppleCare+.

Find My must be enabled when the device is lost or stolen and remain enabled throughout the claim. A deductible applies to each approved replacement.

AppleCare One

AppleCare One combines coverage for multiple eligible products under one monthly subscription. In the U.S., Individual costs $19.99 per month for up to three devices, plus $5.99 per month for each additional device. The base price remains $19.99 even if you enroll fewer than three devices.

AppleCare One Family costs $49.99 per month and covers eligible devices for the subscriber and up to five other Family Sharing members without a per-device charge. It can also cover only the subscriber's devices. Eligible devices are generally added automatically, although some need a check before they can be covered.

Both tiers include theft and loss protection for enrolled iPhones, iPads, and Apple Watches. Individual permits three theft or loss claims in total across the plan every 12 months; Family permits six. Adding devices does not give each one a separate claim allowance.

Apple may require a diagnostic test or inspection before an already-owned device can be enrolled. The device must also be associated with the relevant Apple Account. You can add, remove, or swap eligible devices as your needs change.

available in Australia, France, Germany, the UK, and the U.S. Family is currently available only in the U.S.; prices elsewhere differ.

Plan Prices and Service Fees

Apple offers AppleCare plans for a range of products, but the available plans and prices vary by device and country. AppleCare One Individual is available in Australia, France, Germany, the UK, and the U.S. AppleCare One Family is currently available only in the U.S.

The price of single-device AppleCare+ depends on the product, location, payment term, and coverage offered. There is a one-time purchase option when buying a new device, but Apple also offers AppleCare+ through a monthly recurring payment plan. 

iPhone 18 Pro costs $14.99 per month or $149.99 per year. That premium is paid whether or not you make a claim. Accidental damage service fees are additional to the plan price. These are Apple's current U.S. fees; taxes may apply:


iPhone: $29 for eligible screen-only or back-glass-only damage; $99 for other accidental damage.

Apple Watch: $69 for accidental damage, or $79 for Ultra and Hermès models.

iPad: $29 for screen damage and $99 for other accidental damage.

AirPods and Beats: $29 for accidental damage.

Apple TV: $15 for accidental damage.

HomePod: $39 for accidental damage, or $15 for HomePod mini.

Apple Vision Pro: $29 for damage to an included accessory, or $299 for other accidental damage.

MacBook Neo: $49 for screen or enclosure damage; $149 for other accidental damage.

Other Macs and Apple displays: $99 for screen or enclosure damage; $299 for other accidental damage.



For theft or loss, the U.S. deductible is $149 for an iPhone, $129 for an ‌iPad‌, or $119 for an Apple Watch. These deductibles apply under eligible single-device and AppleCare One coverage.

Express Replacement lets Apple send a replacement before you return the damaged device. It involves a temporary card hold. An iPhone or ‌iPad‌ screen-only claim handled this way is charged at the other accidental damage rate, rather than the $29 screen repair rate.

repair estimator can provide a model-specific iPhone screen repair estimate.

Other Coverage Options

If you are considering AppleCare, it may be worth exploring insurance plans offered by other companies for your device. Many banks, cell phone service providers, and renter's and homeowner's insurance policies cover devices. Some third-party Apple retailers may also offer an extended service plan with your purchase.

Other third-party warranty providers and insurance companies may offer device insurance policies that offer equivalent or better coverage than AppleCare, so it is worth exploring what policies are available for your Apple device in your jurisdiction. Many of these are also available via a monthly subscription and may beat the cost of AppleCare. Coverage for accidents, theft, and loss can vary substantially.

Is AppleCare Worth It?

Whether or not you should purchase AppleCare depends on how you use your Apple device, and how much risk and expense you are willing to take. 

If you are prone to dropping or damaging your device, the argument moves towards adding AppleCare+. Similarly, additional loss and theft coverage will be dependent on how likely you believe you are to lose your device or have it stolen. Ultimately, some users are simply more careless with their devices, and for those people, AppleCare+ is worth it. If you have more than one device you want to protect, AppleCare One is worth considering.

MacRumors feel that AppleCare is worth getting for Apple laptops that you plan on keeping for longer than one year, and iPhone, iPads, AirPods, and Apple Watches due to the accidental damage coverage. For Apple TVs and HomePods, we generally don't see the need, and for desktop Macs and displays it becomes more of a personal judgement call.

title: Apple Planning to Launch Products Faster and More Often
content:
Apple CEO John Ternus is undertaking efforts to restructure the company to accelerate product development and introduce new products more frequently, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. 


Ternus apparently wants Apple to "broaden its range of devices and create a leaner organization with a greater focus on engineering." One proposal under consideration is to rely less on Apple's traditional spring and fall product release cycles, and introduce new devices more quickly and throughout the year. Ternus has also purportedly indicated that Apple must become "more experimental" to remain competitive in the era of artificial intelligence. 

Other plans include eliminating some middle-management positions to reduce corporate hierarchy that separates engineers from senior executives. Ternus believes "Apple should hire fewer people, ask more of its existing engineers, and reduce organizational bloat." During a presentation, he reportedly showed a slide detailing annual headcount growth and argued that the "company should be accomplishing more with fewer employees."

Ternus is also seeking new ways to generate more revenue from existing products amid slowing growth in the company's services business. The launch of new services has also been discussed. To cut costs, early planning meetings for 2027 have seen reductions in planned budget increases, flat staffing levels, and reduced marketing spending.

Gurman cautioned that the changes to Apple's long-standing practices will be challenging and could take years to achieve. There are already indications of changes taking place, with dismissals of directors and engineering program managers taking place in the past two weeks.

Siri, Vision Pro, AI-related software engineering, and Fitness+. Some employees believe that further layoffs are possible later this year and early next year.

title: If you’re not running OS 27, there’s an important update waiting for you
content:
Macworld





If you haven’t gotten around to updating your iPhone or Mac to OS 27, Apple hasn’t forgotten about you. Alongside iOS 27.0.1 and macOS 27.0.1 on Monday, Apple also released an update for older devices that can’t or don’t want to take the leap to OS 27.
You won’t get any new features, but the update patches a pretty serious security flaw for iOS 26, Tahoe, and Sequoia devices. According to Apple’s Security Updates page, 26.7.1 and 15.8.1 for macOS Sequoia contain a single CVE entry that is known to have been exploited:
CoreGraphics
Impact: Processing a maliciously crafted file may lead to arbitrary code execution. Apple is aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27.
Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved bounds checking.
CVE-2026-86950: Meta Product Security
The phrase “extremely sophisticated attack” means most users don’t have to worry. It has historically been used to describe flaws that were exploited to target specific groups of people, such as government officials or journalists. The flaw appears to have been patched ahead of the OS 27 releases, as it is not included in the original release nor as part of the 27.0.1 updates that arrived on Monday. 
To update your devices, head over to System Settings (on a Mac) or Settings (on anything else), select General and then Software Update, and follow the prompts.

Our Verdict 
With the best battery performance we’ve measured from a 10K power bank, genuinely fast 45W wired charging, and a built-in USB-C cable for convenience, the Ugreen MagFlow Pro is a compelling pick—especially if a kickstand isn’t a priority for you.

What is it? A high-capacity power bank with liquid cooling that magnetically connects to your iPhone for up to 25W wireless charging with an integrated 45W USB-C cable and an extra USB-C port for wired power output/input.
Who is it for? Owners of compatible iPhone 16, 17 and 18 models that support 25W Qi2 charging will get the most from it.
Who shouldn’t buy it? Older iPhones (iPhone 15 and earlier) that have wireless charging limited to 15W, and iPhone 14 and earlier that have Lightning instead of the latest USB-C charging port.
25W has become the benchmark for magnetic power banks, even if that top speed is restricted to iPhone 16 and later. If you’re due an upgrade, a 25W charger like this one means you’re covered for faster wireless charging as soon as you trade up.
The Ugreen MagFlow Pro is a 10,000mAh magnetic wireless portable charger that pairs its 25W wireless output with a genuinely fast 45W USB-C port and a built-in USB-C cable—a combination that makes it one of the more versatile chargers we’ve tested. Behind that speed sits Ugreen’s CryoPulse TEC Active Cooling, a thermoelectric cooling module designed to keep the charging surface from overheating during high-power wireless charging.
25W wireless charging generates real heat, and without adequate cooling an iPhone can slow down or even stop charging. Ugreen’s approach to managing that heat is notably more aggressive than most with both a fan and liquid cooling.
Power bank specs
Capacity: 39.2Wh (10,000mAh)
Input charger: USB-C (30W)
Output charger: Wireless (25W) & USB-C (45W)
On test charged iPhone to: 208%
Weight: 8.29oz (235g)
Dimensions: 4.3 x 2.8 x 0.63 inches (108 x 71 x 16mm)
Colors: Gray

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




What is the exact battery capacity of the Ugreen MagFlow Pro?
10,000mAh (10K) remains the largest size you can comfortably clamp to a MagSafe iPhone without it feeling too bulky to pocket. If you want something more compact, a 5000mAh (5K) power bank is worth considering instead but you’ll get fewer recharges from the smaller portable charger. Read reviews of all the best magnetic power banks we’ve tested, both 5K and 10K.
It’s worth noting that not every “10K” power bank has the same actual capacity—watt hours (Wh) is a more precise measure. The Ugreen MagFlow Pro’s 39.2Wh is at the higher end of what we’ve tested and above the average 10K capacity of 38.2Wh.
How fast is the Ugreen MagFlow Pro?
For wireless output, the MagFlow Pro is rated at Qi2.2’s top 25W speed. Only iPhone 16 and later can draw the full 25W; older models, along with the 17e, are capped at 15W, and the iPhone Air at 20W. The difference between 25W and 15W wireless charging is about 15 minutes for the iPhone to reach 50%—30 minutes vs 45 minutes.
The MagFlow Pro’s standout feature is not just its 25W wireless speed. Its 45W USB-C port is matched only by the Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro and Baseus PicoGo AM52 among the chargers we’ve tested. Unlike the Anker, though, the Ugreen includes a built-in USB-C cable (also 45W capable), so there’s no need to carry a separate one—a genuine convenience.
That integrated cable also gives you three simultaneous charging options: wireless, the built-in USB-C cable and the USB-C port. As with most multi-device chargers, though, the total output falls when more than one device is connected—in this case to just 15W. That can still be handy for topping up an Apple Watch or AirPods alongside your iPhone. You can also charge an AirPods case on the wireless charging surface when your iPhone isn’t attached.
Apple now says the iPhone 18 series can reach 50% charge in 15 minutes with a 60W charger (and an iPhone 17 in 20 minutes with 40W), so the high USB-C power output rating comes into its own with the newer iPhones.
Input on the MagFlow Pro is rated at 30W—slower than the Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro’s 45W input, meaning it’ll take a bit longer to recharge the power bank from empty, though that’s unlikely to matter unless you’re in a hurry.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




Is the Ugreen MagFlow Pro’s active cooling effective?
The CryoPulse TEC Active Cooling system is the MagFlow Pro’s defining feature, combining an active micro‑pump, VC copper heat‑spreading foil, and a separated internal layout to circulate coolant directly at the source of heat. Rather than solely relying on passive airflow or a standard fan alone, it uses thermoelectric cooling to actively draw heat away from the charging surface—bringing the center temperature down to reduce heat transferring to the phone.
A copper foil spreads heat across the power bank, and then the liquid layer provides active cooling, before the power bank’s aluminum shell provides more traditional passive cooling.
That cooling power comes with a trade-off: the MagFlow Pro’s 15dB fan is a little noisier than what we measured on the Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro and other portable chargers with built-in fans. It’s not disruptive at a normal working distance, but it’s more noticeable close up, and it’s worth knowing before you decide where to place it while charging. We tested three units to check whether the fan noise was consistent. The third unit was quieter, but we heard a slight buzzing from the other two, so it’s worth noting.
Ugreen claims you can see the active liquid cooling through the power bank’s large screen on its front, but I didn’t really see much going on there—maybe my unit didn’t get hot enough for the liquid cooling to kick in. There’s some movement but you’d have to be bored to watch it for very long. Ugreen says the liquid-cooling system consumes as little as 0.02W, so it shouldn’t noticeably affect charging speed or battery capacity.
How well does the Ugreen MagFlow Pro’s battery perform?
At Macworld we produce a battery performance report for every power bank that passes through our labs, draining an iPhone to 0% and measuring how many charge cycles the power bank can deliver before it’s empty itself.
The Ugreen MagFlow Pro posted the best score we’ve recorded from a 10,000mAh power bank: 208%, ahead of the average 10K score of 174% and slightly ahead of the Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro’s 199%. That’s a strong result, and likely a reflection of how effectively its active cooling keeps charging efficient rather than wasteful through heat. It’s actually a straight tie with Ugreen’s own $79 MagFlow Air Magnetic Power Bank, which is slower at 15W but slimmer at 13.9mm.

				
					

				
			The Ugreen MagFlow Pro (top) is slimmer than its rival Anker MagGo, although a little longer.
Simon Jary




What’s so great about the MagFlow Pro’s design?
At 0.63 inches (16mm) thick, the MagFlow Pro is slimmer than the Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro (0.7 inches/17.8mm), though not as thin as the semi-solid-state Kuxiu S4 power bank (0.53 inches/13.7mm). It’s a touch longer but shallower than the Anker, and at 235g it’s the heaviest of the three we’ve compared here—though that extra weight buys you the integrated USB-C cable the Anker lacks and is definitely worth it (plus who can distinguish a 15g of weight in their hand or pocket?).
The cable can plug into the portable charger’s spare USB-C slot to form a loop that you can use as a handy carry strap.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




Unlike the Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro and Kuxiu S4, the MagFlow Pro doesn’t include a built-in kickstand, so you won’t get the same free-standing viewing angles or StandBy Mode without a separate stand.
The MagFlow Pro is currently available in one color: Gray. It’s compatible with any iPhone from iPhone 12 onward, aside from the MagSafe-less iPhone 16e. If you fancy a similar power bank in more appealing colors, consider the Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro.

				
					

				
			The MagFlow Pro features a color digital display that shows battery info, real-time power, and charging status. It’s a little small but that maintains the power bank’s overall slimness.
Simon Jary




How much does the Ugreen MagFlow Pro Power Bank cost?
The Ugreen MagFlow Pro Power Bank is priced at $149.99 or £109.99, which is at the pricier end of the magnetic wireless power bank market. However, at the time of writing, Ugreen was offering the MagFlow Pro 10K for $99.98 with a coupon, with a similar price available at Amazon.
For more options we have tested and reviewed the best magnetic wireless power banks.
Should you buy the Ugreen MagFlow Pro Power Bank?
With the best battery performance we’ve measured from a 10K power bank, genuinely fast 45W wired charging, and a built-in USB-C cable for convenience, the Ugreen MagFlow Pro is a compelling pick—especially if a kickstand isn’t a priority for you. The active cooling system does its job well, even if the fan runs a little louder than we’d like. If you want maximum charging performance in a slim, cable-included package, this is one of the strongest 10K magnetic power banks around.

title: Baseus PicoGo Air 5K review: The thinnest, lightest iPhone power bank we’ve tested
content:
Macworld





At a glance
Expert's Rating



Pros
Equal thinnest wireless power bank

Available in latest Apple colors
Cons
15W not 25W
Our Verdict 
At just 0.27 inches thick, it’s as slim a magnetic wireless power bank as you can find, and it’s the only ultra-thin portable charger available in Apple’s latest Burgundy color.

What is it? A very thin and lightweight magnetic wireless power bank.
Who is it for? iPhone travelers who want the lightest, thinnest portable charger.
Who shouldn’t buy it? People demanding the very fastest wireless charging.
Apple might not have made its latest iPhone Pro any thinner, but accessory makers are still stripping things down to create the slimmest possible products.
Baseus’s latest range of charging products comes in Dark Cherry – named before Apple settled on Burgundy for the iPhone 18 Pro – and includes a power bank so thin it nearly matches the iPhone Air, plus a 10K power bank and charger in the same color.
Apple’s iPhone Air has a ridiculously skinny depth of just 0.22 inches (5.64mm)—the Baseus PicoGo Air AM71 Magnetic Power Bank is just over a millimeter more, measuring a mere 4 x 2.8 x 0.27 inches (102 x 71 x 6.8mm). Its 0.27-inch thickness is the remarkable part, although we have seen it once before in the BMX SolidSafe Air 5K that matches it in slimness.

				
					

				
			All three colors of the Baseus PicoGo Air on an iPhone Air.
Baseus




Baseus explains that it has a 50% thinner aluminum housing compared to the previous generation, with a 0.35mm charging coil and 0.15mm NFC (used to connect to a dedicated app).
It’s not exactly “card slim” unless you have a metal credit card from the 1980s, but it is certainly more pocket friendly than most power banks. The average depth of a 5000mAh magnetic wireless power bank is a comparatively portly 0.4-inch (10.3mm).
The power bank—also available in Black and Silver, see above—has nice curved edges, making it easy to hold and more visually pleasing.
How does the AM71 compare to other 5K power banks in terms of thinness?
The closest we have measured in terms of slimness are:
Baseus PicoGo Air: 6.8mm
BMX SolidSafe Air 5K (semi-solid state): 6.8mm
Anker Nano 5K MagGo Slim: 8.6mm
Vonmählen Evergreen Mag 5000mAh: 8.6mm
PhoneSuit Elite Mag Slim 5K: 8.9mm
Baseus PicoGo Ultra-Slim 5K: 8.9mm
Kuxiu S2 5K (semi-solid state): 10mm
Infinacore M3 Mini 5K: 10.6mm
The PicoGo Air matches the BMX SolidSafe Air in terms of skinniness. Let’s compare its weight with the same slim power banks mentioned above.
Baseus PicoGo Air: 3.7oz (105g)
BMX SolidSafe Air 5K: 4.1oz (116g)
Anker Nano 5K MagGo Slim: 4.3oz (122g)
Vonmählen Evergreen Mag 5000mAh: 4.34oz (123g)
PhoneSuit Elite Mag Slim 5K: 3.88oz (110g)
Baseus PicoGo Ultra-Slim 5K: 3.77oz (107g)
Kuxiu S2 5K (also semi-solid state): 6.14oz (174g)
Infinacore M3 Mini 5K: 3.88oz (110g)
The PicoGo Air is therefore crowned the lightest power bank we’ve tested, taking that honor from Baseus’s own PicoGo Ultra-Slim. Read more reviews of the best magnetic wireless power banks.

				
					

				
			From the top: Baseus PicoGo Air, BMX SolidSafe Air, and Anker Nano Slim 5K power banks.
Simon Jary




What is the exact battery capacity of the Baseus PicoGo Air?
Power banks are generally classified in milliamp (mAh) hours: 5000mAh as 5K, 10000mAh as 10K, 25000mAh as 25K, and so on.
The Baseus PicoGo Air AM71 is labelled a 5K power bank, as its headline capacity is 5,000mAh, but if we look at the battery capacity in the different measurement of Watt hours (Wh) we get a more accurate view to compare power banks.
The PicoGo Air has a battery capacity of 19.4Wh, against an average 19Wh so a little higher than most. Its slim rival, the SolidSafe Air, has a slightly smaller 18.5Wh capacity, although it did a little better in our recharging tests; which we’ll explain below.
As a comparison, the iPhone Air’s battery is 12.4Wh; the iPhone 18 Pro’s is from 15.86Wh. See our comparison of iPhone battery capacities.

				
					

				
			From the left: Anker Nano Slim, BMX SolidSafe Air, and Baseus PicoGo Air 5K power banks.
Simon Jary




How well does the Baseus PicoGo Air AM71’s battery perform?
In our magnetic wireless power bank lab tests, we let the iPhone’s battery fall to 0%. As soon as the Apple logo has moved to the lock screen we switch to the power bank and see how far it will recharge the iPhone from that near-dead start. This test was performed with an iPhone 16 Pro.
The Baseus PicoGo Air scored 82% in our test, meaning the power bank expired itself with the iPhone registering as 82% charged.
The BMX SolidSafe Air scored 89%, towards the top of the 5K charts despite its lower 18.3Wh rating. That’s probably because it’s a semi-solid-state battery that uses the latest technology to create more durable, safe and long-lasting batteries. That’s not to say the Picogo is none of those things—it just uses the more traditional lithium-ion technology found in most devices, including your iPhone, iPad, and MacBook.
The PicoGo’s 82% is still above average among the many 5K power banks we’ve tested; the average is 77%.

				
					

				
			The Baseus PicoGo Air magnetically attached to the even thinner iPhone Air.
Baseus




How fast is the Baseus PicoGo Air?
The PicoGo Air doesn’t employ the latest Qi2.2 wireless charging standard that can output 25W. Instead, it uses the 15W Qi2 found in most power banks.
A 25W wireless power bank should charge an iPhone from 0-50% in around 30 minutes, while 15W takes about half as long as that again (45 minutes). 15 minutes might not seem a long time to wait, and indeed if you’re not in a hurry it’s no big deal—until you are!
Only the iPhone 16 and later can take the whole 25W, and older iPhones have a maximum 15W wireless charging potential anyway. Remember too that you can connect the power bank to a phone via its USB-C port, which for the PicoGo Air is rated at 22.5W, which any iPhone supports when charging with a cable.
When it comes to recharging the power bank itself, its input rating is 20W.
How strong is the power bank’s magnet?
Baseus warns that as the MagSafe power bank is only 0.27 inches thin, the internal magnet size is physically limited, so the magnetic hold is “somewhat weaker”. It therefore recommends using it without a case on the phone. We didn’t find it too weak when attached to an iPhone in a case, but we report the manufacturer’s recommendation anyway.

				
					

				
			The PicoGo Air (left) is noticeably thinner than the higher-capacity and faster PicoGo AM52, also available in Dark Cherry to match the iPhone 18 Pro and Max.
Simon Jary




Dark Cherry (for Burgundy) range
The PicoGo Air is part of a full Dark Cherry range from Baseus.

				
					

				
			
Baseus




There’s a deeper but higher-capacity 10K PicoGo AM52 Power Bank that is rated at 25W wireless charging and scored 157% in our recharging tests. It comes with an integrated 45W USB-C cable that doubles as a handy carry strap.
You can recharge both with any decent USB-C wall or desktop charger, but Baseus has one in Dark Cherry for you, too: the compact 100W Baseus PicoGo Pro AH22 Fast Charger that’s not as wide (54mm) or tall (52mm) as even your AirPods case (62mm and 47mm), and features a digital display. It has three USB-C ports, each rated at 100W, although 100W is the maximum total output.

				
					

				
			
Baseus




How much does the Baseus PicoGo Air cost?
The Baseus PicoGo Air AM71 has a retail price of $69.99 / £65, but you might find it cheaper on Amazon.
The BMX SolidSafe Air is a little cheaper at $59.99 / £59.99 and boasts the semi-solid-state tech but is not available in the Burgundy color that will appeal to iPhone 18 Pro owners.
Should you buy the Baseus PicoGo Air AM71?
At just 0.27 inches thick, it’s as slim a magnetic wireless power bank as you can find, and it’s the only ultra-thin portable charger available in Apple’s latest Burgundy color. Even in the less interesting Black and Silver hues, it’s a great 5K power bank that will nearly refill your iPhone to 100% and slip into your pocket without you noticing.

title: iPhone Duo Reportedly Facing Production Problems Ahead of Launch
content:
The iPhone Duo is reportedly facing production difficulties ahead of its October launch, with early output expected to be limited.


A person said to be close to Foxconn's supply chain told China's Jiemian News that final assembly yields for Apple's first foldable iPhone were only slightly above 60% as of September 17. The source said that, under Apple's current quality standards, it could take another six months to a year for the assembly line to reach a mature yield. 

According to the source, Foxconn is repeatedly adjusting equipment, assembly processes, and production settings as it makes the ‌iPhone Duo‌ at scale. The source also said suppliers were waiting to see whether Apple would ease any quality requirements to accelerate production. 

Jiemian News said Samsung Display's foldable OLED panels and hinge components had experienced low yields, delayed deliveries, and design changes. Delays in those parts leave the assembler less time to tune its production line.

The publication added that Apple tested Liquid Metal for some hinge parts before reassessing the approach ahead of mass production. Apple says its hinge contains more than 100 components and has a 3D-printed cover.

Jiemian News that Apple's global stocking target for the ‌iPhone Duo‌ in 2026 is approximately six million to eight million units. The publication compared that figure with typical shipments of 20 million to 30 million units over a full product cycle for an individual iPhone Pro or Pro Max model. A separate retail source said Apple's sales guidance exceeds five million units.

MyDrivers claims that one of the device's contract manufacturers asked Apple to choose between prioritizing yield and increasing output. The site suggested that running the production line harder could produce more saleable phones, but with the side-effect of more defective units and higher scrap costs.

unveiled the iPhone Duo on September 9. Pre-orders are scheduled to begin October 16, with availability following on October 23. The ‌iPhone Duo‌ starts at $1,999 in the United States.

title: Best Mac monitors 2026: The Mac compatible displays we recommend
content:

The monitor might be the second-most important part of your Mac’s setup after the Mac, of course–you can’t use any desktop computer without one and even the 16-inch screen on the MacBook Pro feels cramped if you are having a particularly productive morning. Spread your work out by plugging in multiple monitors to your Mac and extending your desktop over a wider space.
Because you’ll spend a lot of time looking at the display, you’ll want to invest wisely. Not only will you want a monitor that provides a pleasing experience, but the quality of the images on the screen can also affect your work.
However, picking a new monitor can be daunting. Not only are there many manufacturers to choose from, but there are also lots of sizes, resolutions, and features to consider—and when we say lots, we mean lots. We’re here to help guide you while you shop, and we have some tips on what to look for in a monitor plus advice on how many monitors each Mac can handle.
Best Mac monitors 2026
These are the best desktop Mac monitors we have tested. We round up the best portable displays for Mac separately if you want to take a larger display out on the road or easily store one out of sight when you’re not using it.
We’ve included Apple’s Pro Display XDR and the Apple Studio Display, not because they are necessarily the best choice, but for comparative purposes.

There are two screen options with this affordable 4K display: matte (MA270U) and glossy (MA270UP). If you want the most vivid radiant picture with deeper blacks and brighter whites, go for the Nano Gloss screen. If you want to banish glare and reflections more so than with the pricey Nano texture glass on the Apple Studio Display, got for Nano Matte.
Some displays sell the stand separately so there’s an additional cost consideration, but that’s not the case here as the stand is included. It offers a great range of adjustment: -5 to 20 degrees of tilt, swivels 15 degrees left or right, and 115 mm of height. The display can also pivot 90 degrees to Portrait mode, a far greater range of motion than the Studio Display. 
The MA270U/P can connect to a Mac through HDMI or USB-C. The USB-C connection offers 90 watts of power so it can charge your MacBook at the same time. If you want to use the display as a connection hub, you need to connect to the Mac via USB-C. Its built-in spare USB-C port offers 15W of power output and the USB-A 7.5W. There are two HDMI ports so you can connect to another device for multitasking.
The one thing that’s immediately noticeable with the MA270U/P is its impressive image quality. Colors are full of life and the detail is excellent. One standout aspect of the image quality is how sharp text appears. This is great for production and design work, but it can even make it more enjoyable to read and write.
It offers image quality that could satisfy users in a production environment–that’s one way of saying that its quality is better than what general users usually get. You might be able to find a 27-inch 4K display that’s a little cheaper, but it won’t look this good.–Roman Loyola
Read the full BenQ MA270UP Monitor review.
The 27-inch BenQ MA270U/P provides a very affordable alternative to Apple’s expensive 5K Studio Display. The BenQ 32-inch MA320U is slightly more expensive, but as well as providing a larger screen it produces a brighter display with bolder, crisper colors, although also at 4K. As a production display, the Studio Display is still expensive but looks affordable compared to the Apple Studio Display XDR. Buyers will enjoy its handsome design, good image quality, and impressive spatial audio, but you can save a lot of money by going with a non-Apple display.
Apple displays have always produced very good image quality, and the Studio Display continues that tradition. Colors are rich, contrast is good, and the brightness is suitable for most tasks.
The Studio Display has a tilt-adjustable stand, but it does not pivot between landscape and portrait modes—a WESA mount beings you a portrait option with the right monitor arm or stand. You can get a stand that provides about four inches of height adjustment but it doesn’t come cheap. The price tag for the tilt- and height-adjustable stand is a whopping $400/£400 more. That Apple stand on its own is about half the price of a comparable third-party 5K monitor with its own height-adjustable stand, such as the BenQ MA270S, reviewed below.
The Studio Display has six speakers (four force-canceling woofers, and two high-performance tweeters) that sound better than most displays we’ve used but are no match for a decent independent speaker.
There’s nothing wrong with this display. Brightness uniformity is good, and color accuracy is excellent. It’s just an old panel, with poor motion clarity from a slow pixel response and a complete lack of modern expected display properties. It’s 2026, and all but the very cheapest monitors have refresh rates over 60Hz, adaptive refresh, HDR, or all of the above.
For a monitor being sold new in 2026, the Studio Display looks like what a nice $999 5K display should. But it costs $1,000 more than that (with a decent stand), and the addition of the webcam, speakers, and Thunderbolt ports doesn’t make up the difference..–Jason Cross

How we test monitors
Macworld staff and other contributors with decades of combined experience have tested the displays in this round up. 
We thoroughly test each monitor, evaluating clarity of the image, maximum brightness, contrast ratio, and color accuracy and color gamut and other aspects of image quality. Motion clarity is also important, especially if the monitor will be used for gaming or other graphical applications.  
We also look at the build quality as well as usability and connectivity, and any special features or modes on offer, especially any that require software that may, or may not work as expected on a Mac. 
Why you should trust Macworld
Macworld prides itself on our experience and expertise when it comes to all things Mac. We conduct in-depth reviews of numerous monitors annually. Our comprehensive recommendations undergo rigorous testing and evaluation by our expert reviewers, who adhere to both performance benchmarks and stringent usability standards.
Should I buy an Apple display for my Mac?
Apple sells displays for its Macs, and you could go with its offerings, which are included above, but its displays are a quite bit more expensive than what third parties offer. 
Buying from a different company may mean you may not get a feature that Apple offers, but it may also be a feature that you don’t need, depending on how you use the monitor. 
There are plenty of companies that have great monitors that you can use with your Mac, without having to take out a second mortgage. Our sister publication PCWorld has tested several displays, and we list their top-rated ones that we have been able to confirm work with Macs, alongside the monitors we have reviewed below. Here are our recommendations in order, starting with Apple’s most expensive.
Are there compatibility issues for Mac monitors?
There are compatibility issues for plain M1, M2 and M3 Macs, which, unlike M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro/Max/Ultra MacBooks, can’t natively connect to more than one external display. Fortunately, there is a solution and we show you how to connect multiple monitors to M1, M2 and M3 Macs in a separate article.
How to choose a Mac monitor
Display technology is a bit of a movable feast, with a lot of confusing jargon and technical features to wade through, as well as a variety of different interfaces and cables that are used by Apple itself and the various monitor manufacturers. So it’s worth taking a closer look at some of the factors that you need to think about when buying a monitor for your Mac.
Screen size
Size isn’t everything, as the saying goes, but it’s a good place to start. Your decision will be influenced by how much desk space you have, and how comfortable you are while using the display. Some people think that a big screen is best, but then when they start to use it daily, they find that it’s too big. And the same goes for customers who think a small screen is best.
If you’re looking for a size to start with for your own personal research, we recommend 24 inches—just like with Apple’s iMac. That seems like a good size for most people, and it’s easy to go up or down from that point. Most people tend to go between 24 and 27 inches for home use.
For professionals—graphics, video, audio, even spreadsheets—a large screen will help you be more productive. Think 27 inches and higher. You’ll be able to fit more elements on the screen and not waste your time scrolling.
If on-screen real estate is valuable to you, consider a multi-display setup. A smaller screen can be used for things like chat, email, web, and more, while the bigger screen is your main workspace. Or get screens of the same size and maximize the space.
Screen resolution
Screen resolution can go hand-in-hand with screen size. Screen resolution refers to the number of pixels used to create what you see on the screen. The higher the resolution, the more detail you can see. Larger displays tend to have more resolution options, as well as the ability to support higher resolutions.
Often, when you find two displays that are the same size but have a wide price difference, it’s mostly because of the screen resolution. Monitors with high resolutions are more expensive. For example, Apple’s $1,599 Studio Display is 27 inches, and it has a high screen resolution of 5120×2880 (5K resolution). On the other hand, LG sells the 27-inch 27UK650-W, but it’s a 3840×2160 (4K) resolution display for content creators, and it’s $350–lower resolution, but $1,249 cheaper. (There actually aren’t other 27-inch 5K monitors available, except for the $1,449 LG UltraFine 27MD5KL-B.)
So what screen resolution should you get? Here are some suggestions; these are guidelines that you can adjust based on your preferences.
For general purpose use, such as web browsing, email, media viewing, small photo and video projects and viewing: 1920×1080 or 2560×1440 (HD)
For more-involved content creation, productivity, and media viewing: 3840×2160 (4K)
For pro-level content creation, productivity, and media viewing: 4K or higher
Want to use an 8K monitor? Read How to connect an 8K display to your Mac.
Connecting a monitor to a Mac
How a monitor connects to a Mac can be confusing. The traditional HDMI and DisplayPort connectors used by many monitors are being replaced–or complemented–by USB-C and Thunderbolt ports. And though USB-C and Thunderbolt cables may look the same, there are actually some important technical differences between them, so it’s important to check which ports your new monitor uses and make sure you buy the correct cables and adapters.
Most recent Mac models have Thunderbolt ports, so if you buy a monitor that has HDMI or DisplayPort interfaces only, then you’ll need an adapter to connect to the Mac. This can get a bit confusing, but Apple does provide a list of the ports included on most recent Mac models so that you can figure out what you need.
Apple also provides a guide to HDMI and DisplayPort technology, which covers Mac models going right back to 2008, so that should provide all the info you need for all the Macs you use at home or at work. Less expensive monitors still tend to use HDMI and DisplayPort, and while it’s not too costly to buy adapters that will allow you to connect your Mac, we reckon it’s worth future-proofing your new monitor by getting one that includes at least one USB-C or Thunderbolt port.
If a display uses Thunderbolt to connect to the Mac, it may have additional USB-C or Thunderbolt ports so the display can act as a hub. In this case, If you have a device you want to connect to your Mac, you can connect it to one of the ports on the monitor, which is already connected to the Mac and probably in an easier location for access.  
Look for a USB-C or Thunderbolt connection with power delivery (PD) that can charge your MacBook. A 65W PD will be enough for a MacBook Air or 14-inch MacBook Pro, but you’ll need at least 90W for a 15-inch or 16-inch Pro.
Read our article on how to connect a second screen to a Mac which explains everything you need to know about how to identify which ports you have, the adapters you will require, and how to set things up.
Ergonomics
If you’re going to spend a lot of time sitting at a desk looking at your lovely new display then you need to keep ergonomics in mind. The ability to tilt the angle of the monitor back and forth, swivel it around for easy viewing, and adjust the height of the monitor in order to avoid an aching back or neck.
Some monitors can pivot or rotate in either landscape or portrait mode.
As a rough guide, there is a point at about 2 to 3 inches from the top of the screen that should be at eye level. Obviously, eye level varies from one person to another, so it’s important that you can adjust the screen for your own personal comfort. You may also prefer a monitor that doesn’t suffer from glare, or you will be forever repositioning the monitor (or your head) to compensate for that.
Other considerations
There are other considerations you’ll want to make when shopping for a monitor. A lot of these come down to personal preference or what you need for the work you do. They include:
Color space (gamut): The number of colors a monitor can show. Professionals need specific color spaces.
Refresh rate: The frequency when a screen is refreshed. Higher rates produce smoother animations.
Webcam: Some displays have a built-in camera you can use for FaceTime and other video conferencing apps, or to record yourself.
Speakers: If you plan on frequently viewing or listening to media, a good set of speakers makes for a better experience.
How many monitors does my Mac allow?
The number of external displays you can hook up to your Mac, depends on its M-series processor. In short, any Pro or Max M1 to M5 processor supports at least two monitors, but base M1/M2/M3 and Neo MacBooks might be limited to just one. See below for the full list and also a link to our tutorial about how to get round the limitations.
• If your Mac has a base (non-Pro or non-Max) M1 or M2 chip, or is the MacBook Neo, it is limited to using just one external monitor unless you follow our DisplayLink workaround tutorial.
• If your Mac has a base (non-Pro or non-Max) M3 chip, it can only use two external monitors if its own lid is closed (so not showing its own screen) unless you follow our tips in the link above.
• If your Mac has a base M4/M5, M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro or Max chip, it is limited to using two external monitors – add up to five using the workarounds.
• If your Mac has an M5 Pro chip, it is limited to using three external monitors – add up to five using the workarounds.
• If your Mac has an M5 Max chip, it is limited to using four external monitors – add up to five using the workarounds.

content:

Top-tier Apple laptops almost never see a big price cut these days, so a $600 discount on one of the most powerful machines defintely caught our eye. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with the M5 Max chip is down to $3,499 right now, a massive savings from its usual $4,099. For pros who need serious muscle, that’s a rare chance to save real money.
This thing is an absolute beast of a computer. The M5 Max chip alone is extremely powerful thanks to its 18-core CPU and 32-core GPU build. Throw in 36GB of memory and a maxed-out 2TB SSD, and you there’s no better combo you could spend money on. Whether you’re editing video, rendering 3D scenes, or juggling a dozen apps at once, the MacBook Pro will keep up with your needs.
Battery life is not something you’ll complain about when it comes to this laptop. If you were to stream video around the clock, you would get a full day’s use on a single charge. The display is stunning, too. The 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR screen can reach 1,600 nits of peak brightness so you can actually use this one outdoors if you wanted to. Plus, colors are particularly vivid, and the blacks look deep. And of course, we love the design, especially the Deep Black color.
Connectivity is amazing too. You get three speedy Thunderbolt 5 ports, a MagSafe 3 charging port, plus Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 for fast wireless. It also supports up to four external displays with the M5 Max, so you can build out a full multi-screen setup.
For $3,499, the M5 Max MacBook Pro is an easy pick if you want one of the fastest, most capable laptops Apple makes.

Whether you’re a Mac desktop or MacBook owner, there’s nothing quite like finding that keyboard that fits perfectly within your setup.
A keyboard, just as with picking the best mice for Mac, is a very personal choice. After all, you’re likely to be pressing its various keys and twirling its dials for hours each day, and that makes getting the investment right all that much more important.
Best Mac Keyboards fully tested
We have all sorts of Mac keyboards in this round-up, including Apple’s default Magic Keyboard with Touch ID and the cheaper, and still-on-sale Magic Keyboard. We have some keyboards with customizable keys and dedicated apps, and wired keyboards (for those fed up with searching for new batteries every few weeks) as well as ergonomic solutions to help you avoid RSI, and some pretty stylish offerings that give Apple a run for its money.
We also look at Hall Effect options that use magnetic sensors to detect key presses, full-size offerings and compact board. Here are our favorite keyboards for Mac users, many of which cost a lot less than Apple’s. Read on to find the Mac compatible keyboard that’s best for you.
You can also use Bluetooth keyboards with iPads, so expect to see some good options here if you are an iPad user, or take a look at our Best iPad Keyboards roundup.
